cultivar: P-126 and other clones, plus seed bushes
processing: Orthodox and tippy black teas alongside a larger CTC output; the orthodox lots are rolled whole, fully oxidised and fired.
harvest_season: First flush clonal lots and second flush lots are both sold; second flush is the classic Assam picking.
appearance_dry: Dark, well-twisted leaf with golden tips in the better grades.
appearance_wet: Bright coppery leaf, fairly even in clonal lots.
taste_profile: Bold and malty, with more complexity than a plain Assam in the better clonal second flush lots.

brewing.notes: Western-style. Try clonal lots without milk first, since that is where the extra complexity shows.

vintage_note: Sold by year, flush and grade, often dated (2023 second flush, 2026 first flush) and sometimes marked as clonal or P-126. First flush is lighter and second flush fuller. Treat it as a tea for the first year or two.
description:
Meleng sits about 10 km from Jorhat on the Meleng River, next to the forest of the Hollongapar Gibbon Sanctuary. Its claim to attention is the P-126 clone, which the owning company traces back to this garden.

Most of its volume is CTC: the company gives around 10 lakh kg of CTC to 4 lakh kg of orthodox. The orthodox share, and especially the clonal and tippy lots, is what reaches specialist shops.

A second flush lot is bold and malty, and tasters of the clonal grades report a bit more going on than in a regular Assam. Brew it in very hot water for about three minutes and go longer only if you plan on milk.

Look for the year and the words clonal or P-126 on the label. They tell you more than a run of grade letters, and they make comparing a first and second flush from the same garden an easy, useful tasting.
history:
The owning company, Jay Shree Tea, says the garden was conceived in 1856 by the planter J.E. Todd, calling it one of the oldest plantations in Assam; another seller gives 1852, and neither date is confirmed independently.

By the company's own account it has won the Tea Board's quality award twice, and clones such as P-126 can be traced to Meleng.
